meta.title: Who really said "Years wrinkle the skin, but to give up enthusiasm wrinkles the soul"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not MacArthur. The line comes from a 'Youth' essay printed under Dr. Frank Crane's name in 1914. MacArthur framed a version of it and later quoted it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Years wrinkle the skin, but to give up enthusiasm wrinkles the soul'?
meta.ogDescription: Not MacArthur. Frank Crane's 1914 essay 'Youth' has the line. MacArthur hung a framed copy over his desk, and later readers credited it to him.

answer.label: Not Douglas MacArthur — actually Frank Crane
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from the essay “Youth,” printed under Dr. Frank Crane’s name in 1914. Quote Investigator ↗ found it in an April 1914 New Mexico newspaper, and the May 1914 Cosmopolitan printing reads “Years wrinkle the skin; but to give up enthusiasm wrinkles the soul.” MacArthur’s connection is a framed version that hung over his desk, which he later quoted.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Carlsbad Argus (Carlsbad, New Mexico), 17 April 1914, p. 8

source.excerpt:
Nobody grows old by merely living a number of years. People grow old only by deserting their ideals.

Years wrinkle the skin; but to give up enthusiasm wrinkles the soul.

Worry, doubt, self-distrust, fear, and despair—these are the long, long years that bow the heart and turn the greening spirit back to dust.
trail: Quote Investigator (2020) ↗: the earliest match it located is The Carlsbad Argus of April 1914, where the essay ran as “Youth by Dr. Frank Crane.” QI concludes that “based on current evidence QI believes that Frank Crane originated this essay by 1914.”

Cosmopolitan, May 1914 ↗: the essay “Youth” runs under the byline “By Dr. Frank Crane,” and the volume index lists it at page 721. It contains the line “Years wrinkle the skin; but to give up enthusiasm wrinkles the soul.”
Home and Progress, March 1920 ↗: the same essay reprinted, word for word, by a bank periodical in Champaign, Illinois. It shows the text was already circulating in periodicals.

Wikiquote, “Youth” ↗: notes that MacArthur quoted the entire piece without attribution on his seventy-fifth birthday (Los Angeles, 26 January 1955), and that it had hung framed over his desk, according to the December 1945 Reader’s Digest.
source.excerptNote: In the popular version the semicolon became a comma. Samuel Ullman’s version of the essay reads “Years may wrinkle the skin, but to give up enthusiasm wrinkles the soul.”

sourceLink.text: Cosmopolitan, May 1914, at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The line is tied to Frank Crane’s essay “Youth,” first published in 1914 (Cosmopolitan, May 1914, confirmed by scan). Works first published in the U.S. before 1931 are now in the public domain.

author.name: Frank Crane
author.heading: About Frank Crane
author.bio: Frank Crane was ordained in the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1882 and was a pastor for more than 25 years. From 1909 he wrote syndicated newspaper columns and books of reflections and advice. His short inspirational pieces were reprinted widely, often without his name, which is how “Youth” came to be credited to others.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: This essay has passed from hand to hand for more than a century, and the credit has moved with it. MacArthur gets it because he kept the text on his wall and recited it. Ullman gets it because his family included it in a book of his verse.

items.why: A version hung framed over his desk. A December 1945 Reader’s Digest piece described it and said it was “based on a poem written by the late Samuel Ullman of Birmingham, Ala.” In 1977 a reader told Ann Landers that “That essay was written by Gen. Douglas MacArthur” (Quote Investigator ↗). He also quoted it without attribution on his seventy-fifth birthday in 1955 (Wikiquote ↗).

Ullman’s version, which reads “Years may wrinkle the skin,” is honored by the Samuel Ullman Museum ↗. QI reports that George Sokolsky traced it to a privately printed compilation that Ullman’s family assembled in 1920. QI judges that “the citations for Crane have precedence” (Quote Investigator ↗).
B. C. Forbes’s Thoughts on the Business of Life credited a condensed version to Phelan, long after Crane’s printings (Quote Investigator ↗).
A California newspaper filler credited an excerpt to Lowe, with the variant “Years wrinkle the face” (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: On current evidence the essay is Frank Crane’s, in print by 1914. MacArthur’s name became attached because he “posted the essay on the wall of his office” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it stuck to MacArthur
lead: MacArthur did more than admire the essay. According to Wikipedia ↗, he hung a framed version on his office wall in Tokyo and often quoted it in speeches, which made the piece better known in Japan than in the United States. When a famous general recites a passage without naming its author, listeners naturally assume the words are his.

A TIME report ↗ on his 1955 seventy-fifth birthday banquet quotes his main address: “You are as young as your faith, as old as your doubt; as young as your self-confidence, as old as your fear.” That line comes from the same essay, and TIME presents it as MacArthur’s own words.
context.detailsSummary: What about the date of Ullman’s version?
detailsBody: Wikiquote’s Samuel Ullman page ↗ heads the poem “Youth (1918)” and gives 1922 as the publication year of From the Summit of Years, Four Score. Quote Investigator, citing George Sokolsky, puts the family’s compilation in 1920. Any of these dates is later than Crane’s 1914 printings, and none of the sources consulted here cites an Ullman-credited printing from before 1914.
